catalog_quote: 1.8.4. Word Stress. HCE also places stress differently than Mainland English at the word level. Notice the following words and where HCE places stress compared to Mainland English. I have indicated the stressed syllable by using bold text for easy identification. Table 1.3 Word Stress in HCE. HCE Word Stress / Mainland Word Stress: hurriCANE / HURRicane; weed WHAckers / WEED whackers; graduATed / GRADuated; townHOUSE / TOWNhouse; chickenFIGHT / CHICKENfight; overcast / OVERcast; moloKAI / MOLokai; stomping GROUNDS / STOMPing grounds; headREST / HEADrest; chinaTOWN / CHINAtown; traumaTIZE / TRAUMAtize; proTEST / PROtest; disCOUNT / DIScount. [p. 130] Jamin maintains the intonation rule in HCE that places the fall on the last stressed syllable, in this case HCE places the stress on grounds. As mentioned in the description of HCE in Chapter 2, HCE places word level stress differently compared to Mainland English. [p. 133] the placement of the stress is on the second syllable of haoleFIED instead of on the first where Mainland English would normally place it. [p. 252] Mainland English speakers would also put the stress on the first syllable in 'graduated', Jamin places stress on the second to last (penultimate) syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Hawai'i Creole English is not in the catalog and this search of works with stress in the title's single title-hit is a false positive: Glottolog ref 447982 (Brenier & Michaelis 2005, 'Syntax-prosody mismatch and copula doubling') was machine-tagged hwc from the keyword 'copula' (Glottolog's record says so); the open author PDF was downloaded and read - it is about the American English 'ISIS' construction in the Switchboard corpus, never mentions Hawai'i, creole or pidgin, and the prosody involved is phrasal prominence on the copula, not word stress. Recommend removing the hwc tag from this reference locally. Beyond the target list, the open-access Drager 2012 overview (downloaded, read) presupposes a stressed/unstressed contrast in Pidgin (vowel quality and non-reduction depend on stress) but states no placement rule, and points to Sakoda & Siegel 2004 'Hawai'i Creole: phonology' pp. 222-223 (Mouton, paywalled, not read) as the primary description - that chapter is the high-priority acquisition for a first-hand stress statement. APiCS survey/structure pages for Hawai'i Creole (checked) contain no stress or prosody feature. No first-hand word-stress placement statement was read in this search of works with stress in the title. Files with.gr, APiCS, Wikipedia) were used.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically assigned as in English (no fixed position is stated), but in many words and compounds it sits further right than in Mainland American English: on the final syllable (hurriCANE, moloKAI, proTEST, disCOUNT), the penult (graduATed, per p. 252 'second to last (penultimate) syllable'), or the right-hand member of compounds (townHOUSE, chinaTOWN, stomping GROUNDS). Rhythm is described as syllable-timed with unstressed vowels unreduced (Carr 1972: 13, 51; Vanderslice & Pierson 1967 via Murphy/Kirtley/Grama; Sakoda & Siegel 2008: 229 via Grama 2015). The nuclear pitch fall of the utterance lands on the last stressed syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for HCE. Carr 1972: 10-11 defines four stress degrees for transcription and notes (p. 13, 51) that in syllable-timed Island speech each syllable carries one of the strong degrees, with weak stress largely absent.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the source gives a contrastive word list rather than a rule, and 'overcast' is listed without a marked stress. Murphy notes Hawaiʻi English (non-creole) speakers use the same 'stress pattern shift' (p. 31, citing Cook 2011).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (single words and compounds) drawn from conversational and podcast speech, plus utterance-level nuclear fall on the last stressed syllable; not citation forms. Not the most authoritative description (Sakoda & Siegel 2008 unreached); Carr 1972 treats a pidgin-to-standard continuum (Types I-V) rather than the creole as a unit.
new_statements.identity_note: Murphy 2013 describes Hawaiʻi Creole English (Pidgin, hawa1247/hwc) from conversational and podcast speakers; Carr 1972 describes a continuum of 'Island English' Types I-V (immigrant pidgin, early creole remnant, 'da kine talk' teenagers, near-standard, Hawaiian standard) rather than the creole as one variety; Kirtley 2014 concerns Hawaiʻi English (the local non-creole dialect, no separate glottocode), summarising Vanderslice & Pierson 1967 for Pidgin.

new_statements.quote: 1. Prosody: the speech rhythm patterns. Pidgin has a syllable-timed rhythm. This is a rhythm in which all syllables in an utterance are said to recur at equal intervals and with stress. This is in contrast to stress-timed rhythm (in languages such as English) in which not all syllables are stressed and only stressed syllables recur at equal intervals of time.
new_statements.citation: Da Pidgin Coup. 1999. Pidgin and education: A position paper. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Department of Second Language Studies
new_statements.locator: Sec. 8 'Pijin nat Ingglish', point 1 'Prosody: the speech rhythm patterns' (unpaginated HTML, dated November 1999; lines 780-785 of the extracted)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File, lines 780-785, reads exactly: '1. Prosody: the speech rhythm patterns / Pidgin has a syllable-timed rhythm. This is a rhythm in which all syllables in an utterance are said to recur at equal intervals and with stress. This is in contrast to stress-timed rhythm (in languages such as English) in which not all syllables are stressed and only stressed syllables recur at equal intervals of time.' (only line-break differences). The same passage is present once in the raw HTML (a full-text search for stress/accent = 1), which is an id_ raw Internet Archive copy of the rtftohtml-2.7.5 page titled 'Pidgin and Educatino', headed 'Pidgin and Education, a position paper, by Da Pidgin Coup, Univer…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Murphy 2013 statement (lexical placement, often later than Mainland English) and does not contradict it, but it contributes no placement rule. It adds a rhythm-type claim (syllable-timed; all syllables stressed) that matches Murphy's own summary of Vanderslice & Pierson 1967 (syllables of equal prominence) and is the source Grama 2015 p. 203 fn. cites for 'Pidgin is syllable-timed'. For the placement question it is effectively silent.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for the position of word stress. The paper only characterises the rhythm: Pidgin is said to be syllable-timed, with every syllable in an utterance recurring at equal intervals and carrying stress, in contrast to stress-timed English. The following 'Phonology' point (unreleased final stops, r-lessness, tense vowels only, pure vowels) says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress; the section only notes general variation between 'heavy' and 'light' Pidgin speakers by age and geographical origin.
new_statements.identity_note: The paper describes 'Pidgin' = Hawaiʻi Creole English generally (it names 'Pidgin (also known as Hawai`i Creole English and Hawai`i English Creole)'), with an explicit caveat that not all features are used by all speakers ('thick'/'heavy'/'strong' Pidgin varies by age and geographical origin). No particular dialect is singled out.

sources.note: Sec. 1.8.4 'Word Stress' (p. 24): HCE places word stress differently from Mainland English, with a 13-item contrastive table (hurriCANE, graduATed, townHOUSE, moloKAI, chinaTOWN, proTEST, disCOUNT..), i.e. stress later in the word / on the right member of compounds; pp. 130, 133, 252 repeat this for graduated (penultimate), haolefied, stomping GROUNDS; nuclear fall lands on the last stressed syllable. Sec. 2.4.3 pp. 48-50 summarises Vanderslice & Pierson 1967: syllable-timed rhythm, syllables of equal prominence in loudness and duration. No general positional rule given.

sources.citation: Drager, Katie. 2012. Pidgin and Hawai'i English: An overview. International Journal of Language, Translation and Intercultural Communication 1: 61-73.
sources.quote: In Pidgin, however, there are no non-prevocalic [r]-colored vowels except for /ɝ/ as in nurse, which in the basilect is found in monosyllabic words or stressed positions (Sakoda & Siegel 2004: 222-223). The vowel in words like north and force are realized without [r] coloring, and the vowel quality depends on stress; it is realized as [ɔ] in monosyllabic words and stressed syllables and as [o] in unstressed syllables. Likewise, unstressed vowels are not realized as [ə] as in comma or [ɨ] as in horses but as a full vowel [ɑ] or [e], respectively.
sources.note: Presupposes a stressed/unstressed syllable distinction in Pidgin (it conditions vowel quality and the absence of reduction to schwa) but gives no statement of where word stress falls. Points to Sakoda & Siegel 2004: 222-223 as the primary phonological description.

sources.citation: Grama, James M. 2015. Variation and change in Hawaiʻi Creole vowels. PhD dissertation, University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa. hdl:10125/50978
sources.note: Instrumental vowel study restricted to stressed vowels. p. 203 fn. reports Sakoda & Siegel 2008: 229 second-hand: unstressed vowels are not reduced to schwa but are full vowels, e.g. English 'alcohol' [ˈælkəˌhɔl] vs Pidgin 'aelkahawl' [ˌælkɑˈhɔl]; notes claims that Pidgin is syllable-timed (Da Pidgin Coup 1999; Vanderslice & Pierson 1967: 157). No positional rule.

sources.citation: Kirtley, M. Joelle. 2014. Prosodic aspects of Hawaiʻi English: The rise-fall contour. University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa Working Papers in Linguistics 45(2). hdl:10125/73251
sources.note: About Hawaiʻi English (the local non-creole dialect); p. 3-4 summarises Vanderslice & Pierson 1967 on Pidgin: 'Pidgin is a syllable-timed language with a wider tessitura than MAE.. emphasis is communicated through duration'; rise-fall contour ends on the final stressed syllable.
